entry.title: The challenge was closed before we started
entry.summary: I had a five-phase plan for a 72-hour challenge before I read the entry window. It had closed 44 days earlier, and the plan was a table of contents rather than a decision.
entry.content:
The challenge closed forty-four days before I read the rules.

Not after I built something. Before I opened the editor. I had the idea, the stack, and a five-phase plan on the table, and the first line of the contest page said the entry period ended on October 5. It was November 18.

The calendar is part of the brief

The challenge was "Hacktoberfest Weekend: Build for a Friend". Entries ran from October 2 to October 5, 2026. Winners were announced on October 9. By the time we sat down, the prize had an owner, the repository window had closed, and the only honest verdict was "not eligible".

That is not a detail you discover in review. It is the first constraint, and it was the one nobody checked. A challenge is a calendar with a theme attached. The theme is the part everyone reads. The calendar is the part that decides whether there is a submission at all.

The second gate

Even with the window open, the post would not have competed. The rules said that non-English submissions were eligible for a completion badge, not for prizes. The draft was in Spanish, written for a local audience. The audience was right and the submission was wrong.

Two gates, both outside the code. Neither one was in the plan. We had spent the thinking on models, embeddings and a local RAG stack, and none of that mattered until those two gates were open.

The plan was a table of contents

The audit scored the plan 9 out of 25. Not because the idea was bad. Because the plan had not made a decision.

"Choose a friend with a private information problem" is a segment, not a person. "A local RAG agent" is the most repeated demo of the last two years. "A lightweight framework" is a placeholder. "Docker or a script" is a fork in the road left open. There were five phases, three data modalities, no cut lines, and one paragraph for writing quality, the criterion weighted most heavily.

The scope was three to four weeks of work in a 72-hour window. PDFs, voice notes, CSVs, embeddings, an agent, verification, Docker, a UI and a handover. Without cut lines, the predictable outcome is that 80 percent is half-built and the post is written at the end, tired, from memory.

A plan that does not choose cannot be executed. It can be improvised, which is a different activity.

What the audit changed

It named the person: Lucía, a freelance photographer with a decade of contracts and invoices she cannot upload. It named one task, one action, one twist: the button that deletes everything, with proof. It put the post in English and gave it 30 to 40 percent of the time. It cut voice notes, CSV and Docker before cutting citations, evaluation, or the friend's reaction.

It also read the judging criteria as a product brief. There were 17 winners across an overall prize, six featured categories and ten partner categories. The original plan had not chosen a category, which is leaving value on the table before the first commit. The rules also said the project had to be new during the entry period, so a repo started earlier would not qualify no matter how good it was.

The most useful part was not the list of fixes. It was the order: eligibility first, then the person, then the one action, then the cut lines, then the stack. The stack is the last decision, not the first.

The writing is the deliverable

The challenge weighted Writing Quality most heavily. The original plan treated the post as documentation to write after the build. That is backwards for a challenge where judges read the post and may never run the repository.

The corrected plan starts the post on the first day, captures screenshots while the thing is being built, and keeps two hours of buffer before the deadline. The post is not a report of the work. It is the work in the form the judge receives it.

That changes what you build. A demo that cannot be explained in one screenshot is a demo that will not score. A twist that needs three paragraphs of setup is not a twist. Writing the post first forces the product to have a shape.

The rule

Read the rules before the roadmap. Check the calendar, the language, the eligibility, and the scoring weights. A challenge is not a prompt; it is a contract with a deadline.

Then make one decision per phase. Who is the person? What is the single action? What is the twist someone will remember? What gets cut when the clock runs out? If a plan cannot answer those, it is not a plan yet.

We did not build for that challenge. We built the audit that stopped us from wasting a weekend, and the corrected plan is still on the shelf for the next window. The cheapest lesson is the one you learn before writing code.

entry.title: Preflight: the gate that listens
entry.summary: Preflight reads what a screen reader actually announces, scores the page by whether someone is blocked, and returns a repair prompt an AI builder can execute. What it does, what it refuses to claim, and why the transcript is the product.
entry.content:
A page can pass every linter and still be unusable.

That is not a hypothetical. It is the default output of an AI builder. The markup is valid, the attributes a checker knows are present, and a blind visitor opens the page and hears a button with no name. Preflight exists for that gap: it reads the page the way a screen reader consumes it, then hands back an instruction a builder can act on.

What the page says

Here is a real page, generated by an AI builder, scanned by Preflight. This is what a blind visitor hears:

  1  document
  2  image                        <- an image with no name
  3  link, Pricing
  4  button                       <- a button with no name
  5  heading, Ship your landing page in minutes, level 1
  6  image                        <- another one

Everything on that page is technically valid HTML. Every attribute a linter checks is either present or reported by axe. And a person using a screen reader cannot tell what those two images are or what that button does.

No attribute-based tool shows you this. Preflight does, because it reads the page the way it will actually be consumed.

The full sequence, from URL to repair prompt, is in What happens during a Preflight scan.

Three layers

The transcript is the first layer. The page is walked with a screen reader and every phrase it speaks is recorded, in order. A role announced with no name is marked and explained in plain language. That is the observation no linter can produce. It is the experience.

The second layer is the verdict. One score that refuses to be green while someone is blocked. A page with 92 findings fixed and one unusable checkout does not get an A. 92/100 but checkout is broken is how a tool gets uninstalled.

The third is the fix prompt. An ordered prompt, ready to paste into the tool that generated the page. Every step names the element, the change, and the announcement the reader must produce afterwards:

## Step 2 - Elements must meet minimum color contrast ratio thresholds
Where: the section #pricing
Affects 2 elements that share this cause. Fix the shared source, not each element:
  - .hero > p
  - footer span
Do: Change the text or background colour. Measured: ratio 1.89:1 (needs 4.5:1),
    foreground #b9bcc4, background #ffffff.
Reader must announce: Re-run Preflight: the contrast rule reports no failing elements.

That last line is the difference between a suggestion and a contract. The builder can verify its own work instead of guessing "looks good to me".

Why the transcript is the product

Most accessibility tooling answers a cheap question: does the markup declare the right things? It can be answered by parsing HTML, and parsing HTML scales. The expensive question is what a person actually hears when they use the component. That requires running the page, in a browser, with assistive technology attached, and reading the output.

The gap between those questions is where the worst bugs live. A live region can overwrite the native announcement and make the experience worse while every attribute stays correct. A tree can render a valid role="tree" with no name and pass an automated audit. A sortable header can announce "toggle button, not pressed" while the table is sorted just fine.

None of those are caught by a rule that asks whether an attribute is allowed. They are caught by listening.

What it refuses to claim

A tool that overclaims is trusted once.

Preflight does not certify anything. Automated checks catch roughly a third of accessibility defects, and every report says so in the body.

The transcript is virtual. It reflects what the DOM declares, not how VoiceOver or NVDA times a specific announcement in a specific browser.

It does not crawl. One URL per scan, by design.

It does not fix your code. It measures, explains, and hands you the instruction. Editing the project is the builder's job, and keeping that boundary is why the MCP server can be called without an approval prompt.

A green score is not compliance. It means no detectable, blocking defect was found on that page at that moment.

Measured, not asserted

The README reports a repair loop, not a demo. Three model families were given the Preflight prompt and their output was re-scanned by the same engine. 95.8% of findings closed, with zero regressions, and both editors preserved every image, link and word on the page. A live product was repaired from 49/100 F to 100/100 A, with every step verified by re-scanning the deployed URL.

That is the part I care about. A scan that produces a score is a thermometer. A scan that produces a repair the builder can execute, and then verifies the result, is a gate.

How it fits the work

Preflight is open source and local-first. The CLI accepts localhost and private addresses by default, because the person running it and the machine being scanned are the same. A hosted server refuses private hosts, so a stranger's URL never reaches the network.

Exit codes are the point: 0 pass, 1 gate failed, 2 scan error. Drop it in CI and a pull request that ships an unusable button stops being merged.

It is built for the sites AI builders produce, where every attribute is present and the page is still unusable. It is also useful on any page where "we ran a linter" has been standing in for "a person can use this".

The rule

Do not ask what the markup declares. Ask what the screen reader says when a person uses the page.

Those are different questions, and only one of them is the product.

If you want a scan, write to gonzoblasco@icloud.com with the URL. The repository is at github.com/gonzoblasco/preflight-a11y.

entry.title: What happens during a Preflight scan
entry.summary: A URL goes in, a real browser renders the page, axe reads the rules, a virtual screen reader walks the accessibility tree, a score refuses to be green while someone is blocked, and a fix prompt comes out.
entry.content:
A scan looks like one action: paste a URL, wait, read a report. Underneath it is a sequence of measurements, and each one exists because a simpler version produced a wrong answer.

This is what happens between the URL and the fix prompt.

1. The URL is checked before anything opens

The first job is deciding whether the scanner should touch the address at all.

A public scan refuses private hosts on the literal address and again after DNS resolution. That second check matters: a hostname can resolve to 127.0.0.1 or a link-local address, and a scanner that follows it becomes a free port scanner for anyone who can call it. The local CLI is different by design. It accepts localhost and private addresses, because the person running it and the machine being scanned are the same. Pass --public-only if you want the strict behavior locally.

Only then does a browser open.

2. A real browser renders the page

Preflight launches Chrome, not an HTML parser. It uses the installed Chrome channel rather than the bundled headless shell, because the accessibility tree of the shell is not the tree users run.

The context is fixed on purpose: 1366 by 900, device scale 1, prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, en-US. A scan that changes viewport or locale between runs is not comparable to the next one. Navigation has a 20 second timeout and the whole scan has a 45 second budget. A page that hangs fails visibly instead of holding a worker.

The page loads with domcontentloaded, then waits for load with a cap, because scanning a skeleton produces findings that belong to the skeleton.

3. Animations are frozen, then the page is allowed to settle

This is the step most tools skip, and it is the source of the false positives that make a score untrustworthy.

Entrance animations are a measured problem. A live React SPA produced three contrast failures that were the page sampled mid-fade at roughly 52 percent opacity. prefers-reduced-motion alone does not fix it, because libraries such as framer-motion animate inline styles and never consult the media query.

Preflight does two things in order. It freezes every animation and transition at its end state, then samples the page until two consecutive visual samples agree. The first is a belt, the second is suspenders. Only then does analysis start.

The result is deterministic: the same page produces the same findings on every run. Without that, a score is not evidence.

4. axe reads the rules

The engine runs axe-core on the stable page, across the rules that apply to the rendered state. That is the mechanical layer: contrast, roles, allowed attributes, names, landmark structure, and the rest of the rule set a mature checker already knows.

Axe is necessary and not sufficient. It answers whether the markup declares the right things. It cannot answer what a person hears when the component is used. The next step is for that question.

5. A virtual screen reader walks the accessibility tree

The page HTML is passed to a virtual screen reader, which walks the tree and records what it announces, in order. Every phrase becomes part of a transcript. A role announced with no name is marked and explained in plain language.

This is the observation no attribute linter can produce. It is also bounded: the transcript reflects what the DOM declares, not how VoiceOver or NVDA times a specific announcement in a specific browser. The report says so.

Content behind interaction is only read if it is open on load. A modal that appears after a click is not in the scan, because the scan does not click.

6. Findings become plain language

Each axe violation is mapped to a rule with three pieces: what the rule means, what the person experiences, and what to change. When a rule has no dedicated copy, a fallback keeps the finding instead of dropping it.

Each finding keeps its nodes: selector, HTML, failure summary. That is what makes the next step possible. A finding without a location is a lecture; a finding with a selector is a repair.

Findings are read twice, and only the ones present in both reads are reported. A consent banner caught mid-mount is a transient state, not a defect of the page.

7. The score refuses to be green while someone is blocked

The score is computed once, in one place, from the findings. The surfaces do not recompute it.

The rule is simple to say and hard to implement honestly: a page with 92 findings fixed and one unusable checkout does not get an A. Blocking defects cap the score. 92/100 but checkout is broken is how a tool gets uninstalled, because the number and the experience disagree.

8. The fix prompt is built from the finding, not from a template

For each finding and each node, the engine builds a step: where the problem is, what to change, the measured cause, and the announcement the reader must produce afterwards.

Two details make it more than a list. The target is inferred from the selector, so the instruction names a component or a shared source instead of a DOM path. And failures that share a cause are grouped under one key, so a CSS variable used in two places produces one repair, not two.

The last line of every step is the contract: re-run Preflight and confirm the rule reports no failing elements. That is what lets a builder verify its own work instead of guessing "looks good to me".

9. The loop closes by scanning again

A report is not the end of the process. The repair prompt is applied, the page is scanned again, and the new score and transcript are the evidence. The README reports a live product repaired from 49/100 F to 100/100 A this way, with every step verified by re-scanning the deployed URL.

That is the difference between a thermometer and a gate. A thermometer tells you the temperature. A gate tells you whether the thing can ship, and what to do before it does.

What it deliberately does not do

It does not certify. Automated checks catch roughly a third of accessibility defects, and every report says so.

It does not crawl. One URL per scan, by design.

It does not fix your code. It measures, explains, and hands you the instruction. Editing the project is the builder's job.

It does not replace a person with a keyboard and a real screen reader. It narrows where that person should look.

One engine, several surfaces

The same engine runs behind the CLI, the GitHub Action, the web report and the MCP server. The MCP tools are read-only by design, so a hosted builder can call them without an approval prompt. The score, the rule copy and the limits travel with every observation. A surface that recomputes the score is a bug, not a feature.

The point of the architecture is not elegance. It is that the thing you run locally and the thing a builder calls remotely cannot disagree about what the page says.

entry.title: The Quieter Announcement
entry.summary: I fixed a screen reader bug by deleting an announcement. React Spectrum's live region was overwriting what VoiceOver already said natively, and no linter could see the collision.
entry.content:
I once fixed a screen reader bug by deleting an announcement.

That sounds backwards, and it is the point. On the surface, the change was small: 41 lines added, 80 removed, one hook, two test files, merged into Adobe's React Spectrum in October. What it revealed is that most accessibility work is aimed at the wrong target.

What the user heard

A ComboBox with sections. You open it, you arrow down through the options. VoiceOver, on macOS and iOS, speaks each item as you move through it: the label, the role, the position, and whether it is currently selected.

That is a rich announcement. It is also, in a very literal sense, a gift. The browser and the screen reader cooperated to produce it.

Then React Spectrum overwrote it.

The useComboBox hook carried a workaround, and the comment above it explained why it existed:

// VoiceOver has issues with announcing aria-activedescendant properly on change
// (especially on iOS). We use a live region announcer to announce focus changes
// manually.

An aria-activedescendant pattern moves focus in the accessibility tree without moving real focus. Some screen readers historically did not follow that movement reliably, so the library announced each change by hand, through a live region, to be safe.

The workaround was correct when it was written. It stopped being correct when VoiceOver started announcing per item details natively. And once both things were happening at the same time, they did not cooperate. They competed.

The live region fired on every focused item change and replaced the native speech with a single string: the item name. So instead of hearing "Pricing, menu item, 3 of 12, selected", a user heard "Pricing", and then moved on.

Less information, delivered more urgently. Which is the definition of a regression that hides.

Why nothing caught it

Run that page through axe. Everything passes.

The combobox has the right role. aria-expanded is synced. aria-controls points at the right listbox. The options carry aria-selected and aria-posinset, and the aria-setsize matches. The live region exists, is not hidden, and is not empty. Every attribute a linter knows how to check is either present or not applicable.

The bug lived somewhere no linter looks: in the collision between two things that were each individually correct.

Accessibility, at that layer, is not a property of the markup. It is a property of the runtime, and more specifically it is a property of what a person actually hears. Markup is the input to that. It is not the thing itself.

The fix

The announcement was still needed for one narrow case: moving into a new section, where VoiceOver stays quiet and the section title and option count would otherwise be lost. So the gate became the section, not the item.

if (isGroupChange) {
  const announcement = stringFormatter.format('focusAnnouncement', {
    isGroupChange: true,
    groupTitle: sectionTitle,
    groupCount: section ? [...getChildNodes(section, state.collection)].length : 0,
    optionText: focusedItem['aria-label'] || focusedItem.textValue || '',
    isSelected
  });

  announce(announcement);
}

Everything else stays silent and lets the platform speak. Arrowing through a section: native speech, intact. Arrowing to the selected item: native speech, intact. Entering a section: one manual announcement with the section title and the option count, then out of the way.

The review was the hard part, and it was the interesting part. I had updated the combobox tests to assert that per item navigation no longer triggers a manual announcement. The maintainer pushed back twice. The first version, in their reading, was not.toHaveBeenCalled wearing a costume. The second round asked what those tests covered that nothing else did. The answer, eventually, was nothing. Once the announcement moved to section changes, the tests had nothing left to assert, and they were removed. The suite ended at 259 tests across two packages.

I shipped a smaller diff than I opened, and the PR was better for it. That is not the instinct most people have.

The second failure, which was mine

A month earlier I had merged a test only PR into the same repository, locking in that aria-posinset stays global across menu sections. Four items across two sections must count 1 through 4, matching aria-setsize=4. If a section restarts the count, a screen reader announces "item 1 of 2" when the truth is "item 1 of 4".

React Spectrum was already doing it right. Nothing guaranteed it. So the test was there to make sure a future refactor could not quietly break it.

My first version of that test was worthless.

The helper I used to build the fixture flattened the sections into a plain list of items. The DOM that the test rendered never contained the sectioned structure the test claimed to cover. It went green. It was decoration. A maintainer spotted it in seconds.

The corrected version renders each section through the real hook, including labelled groups and their headings, and also covers the section without a heading, where the accessible name comes from aria-label.

Two PRs, two different mistakes, and the same root cause: I was reasoning about the model in my head instead of the artifact that ships. In the first case I trusted the attribute over the announcement. In the second I trusted the fixture over the DOM.

The rule I kept

If you want to know whether a component is accessible, do not ask what attributes it has. Ask what a screen reader says when a person uses it. Those are different questions, and only one of them is the product.

Most tooling answers the first question, because the first question is cheap. It can be answered by parsing HTML, and parsing HTML scales. The second question requires running the thing, in a browser, with an assistive technology attached, and reading the output. It does not scale nearly as well. It also happens to be the only one that predicts what a blind user experiences.

That gap is what I ended up building a tool around. Preflight loads a page in a browser, reads its accessibility output the way a screen reader consumes it, and reports what is actually announced rather than what is merely declared.

The demo page in its README has every attribute in place, and two unnamed images and an unnamed button. Valid HTML, clean lint, unusable.

PRs: adobe/react-spectrum#10503 and #10554.

entry.title: The bug jsdom could not see
entry.summary: A shadcn/ui PR sat for three months while 61 jsdom tests passed. jsdom does not fire scroll events for programmatic scrolls, so it could not see the spacer collapse the fix introduced. Browser tests found that and two more bugs.
entry.content:
A PR I opened in August merged on November 2. For most of that time, 61 tests passed and the code was wrong.

Not in a corner nobody visits. MessageScroller is the primitive behind the streaming chat example, the one where a reply types itself into the page while you watch. The bug lived in the second after you scroll.

A scroll during the answer

When a user message anchors near the top of the viewport, the component reserves room below it: a tail spacer, sized so the reply has somewhere to grow without pushing the page. As chunks arrive, the spacer is consumed and the reader stays where they are. That is the whole design.

Then the reader scrolls. Up, usually, to re-read the question. A manual scroll releases the anchor, and from that moment the spacer has no owner.

With autoScroll on, follow mode re-arms on the next commit and scrollToEnd drives the spacer to zero in a single frame. The reserved room collapses and the viewport jumps to the live edge while the reply is still three lines tall. With autoScroll off, nothing re-arms, the spacer freezes at its current height, and a dead gap sits under the reply. The answer can grow to fill the screen and the gap does not move.

Same gesture, two failures, one cause. Scrolling to read while an answer arrives destroys the room reserved for the answer.

The test that could not fail

reconcileFollowMode had a branch that re-armed following-bottom whenever autoScroll was on and the scroll was not at the end. It excluded two modes, settling-jump and anchored-to-message. It did not exclude free-scrolling, the mode a turn sits in after the reader grabs the scroll.

The second half is geometry. scrollable.end is measured against contentBottom, and contentBottom does not include the tail spacer. A reader parked inside the spacer reads as being at the end, so their own gesture flipped them back into following. The next chunk called scrollToEnd and one frame later the room was gone.

The other gap was simpler: a released spacer was never drained. scrollToEnd consumed it on the follow path, and nothing else touched it.

I wrote the fix and a regression test. The suite went to 61 passing, typecheck clean, and I opened the PR.

The first review

daltino read the drain logic the next day and asked one question: what happens if the stream stops before the spacer reaches zero? The guard I had added, spacerHeight === 0, would then block follow mode from ever re-arming. The test only exercised the happy path where the stream runs long enough to drain the room.

That reading was right, and the edge case was the interesting one. A stream is not a promise. It can end mid sentence, mid drain, with a few pixels of reserved room left and no further resize to consume it.

I pulled the drain into drainReleasedSpacer and ran it from two places: handleResize when the reply grows into the room, and syncAfterScroll when the reader moves. A scroll to the real bottom then finishes the job, because the bottom includes the spacer. I added the test that cuts the stream.

At that point the code did what I thought it should do. It still was not mergeable.

What jsdom cannot see

shadcn reviewed on September 2 and named the thing no test in my suite could have named: syncAfterScroll runs on every scroll event, including the programmatic one that places an anchored turn. In a real browser with autoScroll on, every anchored turn got yanked to the bottom. The exact bug the PR existed to fix, reintroduced by its own fix.

The 61 tests passed because jsdom does not fire scroll events for programmatic scrolls. The handler never ran. The test was not weak or badly written. It was measuring a page where the event does not happen.

Two smaller problems sat in the same function. On resize, a reader who had scrolled up past the spacer zone produced consumed equal to zero, so the spacer collapsed and scrollToEnd yanked them out of the transcript they were reading. On scroll, the drain subtracted an absolute overlap on every event instead of a delta, so inertial scrolling over-drained and cascaded into a jump.

The revision skipped anchored-to-message, settling-jump and the programmatic scroll flag. It recomputed the room from absolute geometry on every event, max(0, contentBottom + spacerHeight - (scrollTop + clientHeight)), so repeated events converge instead of compounding. It returned early when the reader was above the spacer zone, and handed off to scrollToEnd only at the real bottom, where the spacer is zero by construction. Then two browser tests with autoScroll on: one asserts that placing an anchored turn does not yank, the other that a manual scroll drains the spacer without moving the reader and that scrolling to the bottom re-engages following.

jsdom passed 51 of 51. Browser mode passed 48 of 48.

What green means

I got the diagnosis wrong too, before any of this. On August 3, sandengocka described both changes in the issue thread with the reasoning intact. I answered that main already covered it in #11106. It did not.

That fix ran while the turn was still anchored-to-message; this bug lives in what happens after a manual scroll knocks the turn out of that mode. I went back through the code, confirmed their reading, and wrote the PR on top of it.

A green suite is a statement about an environment, not about the product. jsdom is honest about the DOM and silent about what a browser does while it scrolls, and the gap between those two is exactly where a spacer, a scroll event and a single frame can ruin a reading experience.

Test where the bug lives. Three months, four files, 346 added lines for one deleted one, and what unblocked it was a test that a different runtime could actually run.

entry.title: The dialog description that never arrived
entry.summary: Carbon's ComposedModal forwarded a title but no description, so screen readers announced a dialog with no clear purpose. The PR added aria-describedby, and review caught a test that proved only the attribute.
entry.content:
A dialog opens and the screen reader says its title. Then nothing.

No sentence about what the dialog wants, what happens if the user continues, or what they are agreeing to. Just a name, and a decision to make without context.

A name is not a description

A label answers which thing this is. A description answers why it is here and what it will do. In ARIA they are two attributes with two jobs: aria-labelledby points at the title, aria-describedby points at the sentence that follows it.

Most dialogs in a design system get the first and skip the second. The title is visible, so someone wires it up. The body text is visible too, but nobody connects it to the dialog element, so it stays text on a screen.

A sighted user reads it in passing. A screen reader user hears the name and then goes hunting through the dialog for the rest.

That hunt is the bug. It is not a missing attribute in a validator's sense. It is a dialog that names itself and explains nothing.

The description was sitting in the dialog the whole time. The problem was never absence. It was attachment: the sentence existed on screen and was not part of the thing that receives focus.

The escape hatch was closed too

Carbon's ComposedModal carried that gap for months. Issue #21342, opened in January 2026 against @carbon/react 1.93.0, described it without drama: the component supported aria-label and aria-labelledby, and not aria-describedby.

The usual workaround for a missing prop is to pass the attribute anyway and let the rest spread carry it. That door was shut. ComposedModal spread its remaining props onto the outer wrapper, not onto the element carrying role="dialog". The attribute would land on a div that no assistive technology treats as the dialog.

The reporter also named the inconsistency. The plain Modal already handled this through its alert prop, wiring aria-describedby to the modal body. The composed variant, the one with a header, a body and a footer, had no equivalent. A confirmation dialog built out of it could be perfect in every other respect and still say only its title.

So I opened a pull request with an optional prop, forwarded to both render paths: the native <dialog> element when enable-dialog-element is on, and div[role="dialog"] when it is not.

The test that proved forwarding

The first review asked for a test. Fair. The change added a code path and shipped no coverage for it.

I added two. One covered the fallback div[role="dialog"], following the pattern of the existing aria-label tests. One covered the native dialog behind the feature flag. Both ran across the three ComposedModal variants in the suite.

I reported 118 tests green.

Then adamalston read the test instead of the badge.

The test referenced description-modal-id without rendering that element. It checked that the attribute arrived on the dialog. It never checked that anything on the page was being described.

That is the original bug, restated one layer down. aria-describedby is an id reference, and nothing validates the target. A dialog can point at an element that was never rendered and the DOM will accept it without complaint. The test asserted the part that already worked and never touched the part that mattered.

A green check told me the attribute was forwarded. It could not tell me the dialog had a description. Those are different claims and I had been treating them as the same one.

The branch I broke

While applying that feedback, I force pushed a broken state. The test file ended up with corrupted JSX, and the changes I described in a comment were not actually in the branch. adamalston noticed before I did: "Uh? Did you review your changes before requesting another review?"

He was right, and the answer was no. I had described the fix from memory of the diff, not from the file.

I rebuilt the branch, rendered the description element next to the modal, and let the test ask for the accessible description instead of an attribute. The ComposedModal suite passed at 142 tests.

The same review had two smaller points. The JSDoc mentioned cds--modal-container, an internal class name, and read as if the prop only applied to the div path. It now says "Specify the accessible description for the modal." On the final pass he caught a propTypes comment that did not match the interface, marked resolved without being addressed.

The merged change is 63 added lines and one removed across three files. The prop stays optional and does the only thing it can:

<ComposedModal aria-describedby="delete-note">
  ...
  <p id="delete-note">This removes the workspace. It cannot be undone.</p>
</ComposedModal>

The component does not invent a description. It cannot know what the modal is for. It just stops dropping the sentence the caller already wrote.

The rule

Render both ends of a relationship before you assert it. A test for an id reference that never renders the target is a test of the plumbing, and plumbing that ends in a wall looks identical from the valve.

And a name is not a description. One says what opened. The other says what it will do. A dialog with a title and no description is a sentence missing its verb: the user hears the subject and has to guess the rest.

entry.title: Sortable headers are not toggle buttons
entry.summary: A sortable Datagrid header announced itself as a toggle button, because aria-pressed competed with aria-sort and won. Removing the attribute let the sort direction reach the user again.
entry.content:
Sorting a column is one action with three outcomes. The control that did it was announcing two states, and neither of them was the sort.

The table was a Datagrid with sortable columns. I tabbed to the first sortable header and pressed Enter. An arrow appeared, the rows moved, the order changed on screen. VoiceOver said "toggle button, not pressed".

I activated it again. The arrow flipped to the other direction, the rows reversed, and the announcement came out in the same shape. Pressed or not pressed. Nothing about up or down.

A blind user sorting that table has no way to know whether the list is now A to Z or Z to A. The rows are in a different order and the only feedback is the absence of a state that never meant anything.

The header cell was already saying the right thing. aria-sort lives on the columnheader element and carries ascending, descending or none. The problem was the thing in the tab order. The focusable element was the button inside the cell, and the button had its own role and its own state, and that is what got read.

Pressed is not sorted

aria-pressed does not describe a button. It assigns one. The moment a button carries it, the element is a toggle button, and assistive technology reports it as a two-state control with an on and an off.

Sorting is not two states. It is three: ascending, descending, and neither. Even in the best case, mapping three outcomes onto a boolean throws information away.

In practice it was worse than that. false meant "this column is not the sorted one", which a listener hears as "the toggle is off", not as "this table is sorted by something else".

The value came from a helper called getAriaPressedValue. It took the column, read isSorted, and returned 'true' or 'false'. Four lines, defensive null check, correct TypeScript, and the wrong question.

Why nothing caught it

Issue #9839 came in from someone using macOS VoiceOver, with the IBM Equal Access checker listed as the automated tool. That combination is the whole lesson. The automated checker ran, and the markup was valid.

A button may carry aria-pressed. Nothing in the rules says a sortable header may not.

A linter can tell you whether a role allows an attribute. It cannot tell you whether the resulting announcement describes the thing on screen. Between valid and usable there is a gap, and only a person with a screen reader stands in it.

The test suite had the same blind spot from the other side. All 47 tests in Datagrid.test.jsx passed, and they were testing sorting: click the header, assert the row order changed, click again, assert it reversed. Those tests prove the sort works. None of them asked what the sort sounds like.

The behavior was covered. The announcement was not.

The fix was a deletion

I removed aria-pressed from the Button in useSortableColumns, and deleted getAriaPressedValue with it. The sort state stayed where it already was, on aria-sort in the columnheader, computed by getAriaSortValue in DatagridHeaderRow. Two files, 24 lines added, 11 removed, most of the additions being a comment that points at the issue.

What made me confident this was the right shape rather than a guess: the core @carbon/react DataTable does not put aria-pressed on its sort trigger at all. Its TableHeader leaves the state on aria-sort. Datagrid was the outlier, not the reference. The fix was not a new convention, it was deleting an extra one.

The regression test reads the first row, collects the columnheaders, finds the button inside each sortable one, and asserts getAttribute('aria-pressed') is null. On main the same assertion finds "false" and fails. Merged on October 7, after one dismissed review and two approvals.

The hole I left

The assertions sit inside an async callback passed to Array.from(...).map. Nothing awaits that array. A failed expectation there does not surface as a named failing assertion, it surfaces as an unhandled rejection somewhere else in the output. The test can go red without telling you which column broke.

I found it rereading the diff, later than I would like. The habit that would have caught it is the one I keep relearning: assert on the element that carries the semantics, and make the failure point at it. Same rule as the test, applied one level up.

There is a second limit, and no test fixes it. An absence assertion proves the attribute is gone. It cannot prove the direction is announced.

That check is a person, headphones on, sorting a table. It was a person who found this in the first place, which is the right order of events and the wrong one to rely on.

The rule

aria-pressed is a role assignment wearing the costume of a state. Set it and the control is a toggle, no matter what else the markup says.

When two attributes describe the same thing, put the state on the element that carries the meaning, not on the element that happens to receive the click. The header cell carries the column. The button carries the action. aria-sort belongs to the column.

And the cheapest fix is often a deletion. Nothing was added to make this table announce correctly. One attribute and one helper stopped being there, and the semantics that were already present became the only thing left to hear.

entry.title: Focus after the step changed
entry.summary: Pressing Next in CreateFullPage sent focus to the skip link: the helper looked for an inert attribute the component never set. One querySelector for the visible step class fixed it, and a focus assertion that had never existed.
entry.content:
The bug report said focus was lost. It was not. It was delivered, with confidence, to the one element that undoes the step you just took.

A keyboard user presses Next in a multi-step form and expects to land inside the step that just appeared. In CreateFullPage, focus went to the "Skip to main content" link at the top of the page instead.

Picture the screen reader announcement. The user activates Next, the form swaps content, and what they hear is a link at the top of the document whose only job is to jump past the navigation. Nothing announces the new step. Nothing says the form moved on.

A keyboard-only user pays in keystrokes. From the skip link, the way back to the form is tab, tab, tab through everything above it. The user who cannot see the page has no way to learn the new step ever rendered, and the announcement actively tells them they are at the beginning.

Same bug, two bills.

The step that was never inert

A helper called getActiveStep() walked every step in the DOM and returned the first one whose ancestor chain carried no [inert] attribute. In the abstract the logic is sound: the visible step is the one that is not inert.

CreateFullPageStep never sets inert. It hides the inactive steps with a class, __step--hidden-step, which is display: none, and marks the active one with __step--visible-step. So the walk returned the first step in DOM order every time, whichever step was actually active.

The hook then did a reasonable thing with the wrong container. getFocusableElement queried it for button, input, select, textarea, a[href], took the first enabled match, and called .focus() after a 10 ms wait.

That wait mattered later. TearsheetShell needs a timer to claim focus during a stack change, so the focus call never runs on the same tick as the render.

The element it found was real. querySelectorAll finds elements inside a display: none subtree without complaint. .focus() on one of them is a browser no-op.

Find the wrong step, find a genuine input inside it, ask the browser to focus something it cannot focus, get silence. Focus stayed on the Next button or fell to <body>, and the next tab stop collected it.

Why the tests were green

The file had 27 tests before mine. Not one of them read document.activeElement. They asserted that step two became visible, that onNext was called, that the progress indicator moved. The state was covered, the side effect was not.

The helper was also right just often enough to hide. When the active step is the first in DOM order, "the first step without inert" and "the visible step" are the same element. Any test that stayed on step one, or supplied a working firstFocusElement selector, got the correct answer by accident.

And the bug lived behind a timer. Even a test that watched focus would have needed to wait for it. Async with no assertion is invisible twice.

This is the part I did not appreciate until the test failed: a green suite does not mean the behavior was checked. It means the assertions that exist passed. Focus management was simply not among them.

Query the thing itself

The fix is one line, and it is not clever. Stop inferring visibility and read the class the component already writes.

const getActiveStep = () => {
  return document.querySelector(`${blockClass}__step--visible-step`);
};

The visible-step class is how the component decides what a user sees. Reading it back is not a shortcut around the abstraction, it is the same source of truth the render already trusts. It is also one query instead of a walk up every ancestor of every step.

There is a trap in that selector worth naming. blockClass already ends in __step, so appending __step--visible-step produces ...__step__step--visible-step. I left the doubled form in a comment in the hook so the next person does not tidy it away.

I kept the isNotContainedInInert check. useCreateComponentFocus is shared with CreateTearsheet, whose steps do set inert on the outer element as well as the visible class. Both paths still resolve, and I put that blast radius in the PR description before review rather than after.

The regression test renders two steps with real inputs, clicks Next, and asserts that document.activeElement is the input inside the visible step, and is not the skip link, and is not the body. It fails on main with a waitFor timeout. The suite went to 28 of 28.

The deprecation review

The first review approved the change and told me the component is on the deprecation list. There is an example pattern in StackBlitz now, and the advice was to copy that into the application and maintain the fix there.

That is a fair argument in a roadmap sense, and it is not the one that settles this. The bug is live on the published package for everyone in the range the issue tested, 2.44 through 2.80. The change is one line in a shared hook plus a test, with no new API surface. Someone who upgrades today gets working focus without migrating first.

I said that in the thread and offered to open a separate PR against the example if the pattern turned out to carry the same step-change logic. Two maintainers approved it and it merged on 14 September.

The rule

A helper that decides what is visible has to read what the component actually writes. An attribute nobody sets is not a weak signal, it is a constant, and a constant will return the first element forever without ever throwing.

The second rule is about the test. If the behavior is focus, assert on document.activeElement. A test that only checks which step carries the visible class will stay green while every keyboard user lands on the skip link to start over.

entry.title: Counting items across sections
entry.summary: A test-only PR locks in that aria-posinset stays global across menu sections. The first version flattened the fixture, went green and tested nothing; the corrected one renders the real sections.
entry.content:
A green test is not evidence. It is a claim with a check next to it, and the check only covers the code the fixture actually reaches.

Most accessibility work produces that kind of test by accident. The fix is real, the assertion is real, and the fixture quietly walks around the part that was broken.

This is the story of one of mine.

First, the announcement

In January, tomsontom filed issue #9556 against the Picker sections example. The first item in the popup, Chocolate, reported aria-posinset=2 while the list reported aria-setsize=6.

Two numbers, one object, no agreement. The first option in a menu is item one. A screen reader was saying "2 of 6" before the user had moved.

The cause was a mismatch between two attributes computed from different sources. aria-setsize used the global item count. aria-posinset came from item.index, which restarts at zero inside each section. The numbering started over in every group while the total stayed global.

What that sounds like is worse than a wrong number. A reader moves into the second group and hears "1 of 6" for an item that is actually item four. The position is the only cue about how far through the list you are, so the list reads as two short lists instead of one long one.

The fix landed in PR #10487. A shared helper, getPosInSet, counts items globally and ignores section headers. It went into both useOption and useMenuItem, because the same pattern lived in the listbox and the menu.

After that, the values were correct. Nothing kept them correct.

A test that only guards what it renders

My next PR was test-only: test: add regression for global aria-posinset across sections. One file, 102 lines added, 2 removed. The idea was simple. Render a menu with two sections and four items, assert that the positions are 1, 2, 3 and 4, and assert that aria-setsize says 4.

My first version passed.

It also never built a section. The helper I wrote to create the mock flattened the groups into a plain list of items, so the hook received four siblings and no group structure at all. The section code never ran. The section branch that had caused the bug in the first place was not in the test.

With a flat list, index and position are the same number. Four items produce 1, 2, 3, 4 whether the logic is right or wrong, because there is no section to restart anything. The test agreed with itself.

snowystinger reviewed it and wrote one line: "The test isn't rendering the sections." Then, in the same comment, the part that stung: "while that shouldn't affect the posinset, it's incomplete."

That is exactly right, and it is the reason the review mattered more than the test. The numbers were correct. The coverage was zero.

What a real fixture looks like

The corrected helper renders each section the way the component does. A role="presentation" wrapper holds a role="group" inside it, and the group is labelled by its section heading through aria-labelledby.

The assertions changed shape too. Before checking any number, the test verifies that both groups exist and that each one is labelled by its own heading. The DOM structure is part of the regression, not a stage set for it.

Then the positions are checked, and then aria-setsize, and then that the two agree. Five assertions in useMenu.test.tsx, all passing, full lint clean.

Asserting the structure first is not ceremony. If the groups disappear, the position check should fail for that reason and not for an unrelated one. The failure message then says which part broke.

The difference between the two versions is one helper function. The difference in what they cover is the entire bug.

The part I did not fix

The second review asked for two more things. The heading span needed to render node.rendered, matching the real MenuSection, so the visible text and the labelling come from the same source. That was a small change.

The other request was to move the test up a level, to react-aria-components with a real Virtualizer. I tried. I found something I did not expect: with the virtualizer in the tree, aria-posinset resets per section in the rendered output. The second section starts again at 1 instead of continuing at 3.

The hook contract holds. The layout path does not carry it through.

That is a separate bug with a separate fix, and folding it into a test-only PR would have muddied both. I kept the test at the hook level, where the original contract was verified, and left the virtualizer behavior as a note on the PR. It has no follow-up issue yet, and that is a loose end I am aware of.

How to tell a test is decoration

There is a cheap check, and it takes a minute. Break the thing the test claims to protect, and run it. If the test stays green, the test is describing the fixture, not the behavior.

The other check is structural. Read the setup and ask which lines of production code it can reach. A test that builds its own simplified world can only fail when that world breaks, and the real one is usually somewhere else.

A number in an assertion is not proof of anything on its own. It is proof when the structure that produces the number is also in the test. Otherwise it is a coincidence with good formatting.

The PR is merged. Four items, two sections, positions 1 through 4, matching a set size of 4. That took five assertions and one honest review.

entry.title: Orchestrating a 10,000-line refactor
entry.summary: A 10,000-line macOS app spread across three giant files became a modular structure through four stages kept apart: planning, execution, cross-review by a different model, and verification. The public API never moved.
entry.content:
Refactoring 10,000 lines of monolithic code is not a writing problem. It is an orchestration problem.

The code did not need to be smarter. It needed to move without breaking anything that depended on it.

Three files, one surface

The app was a macOS cleaner. Ten thousand lines lived in three giant files, with routes, utility code and business logic interleaved. A change to a path rule meant scrolling past the route table to find it, and the route table was the thing most likely to break.

The hard constraint was external. The frontend called the app through a public API, and that API could not move. A modular structure that renamed a response field would have forced a second refactor on the client. So the job had one non-negotiable: the surface stays identical while the inside is rebuilt.

That constraint changed the shape of the work. The task was not "improve this code". It was "prove the behavior did not change while the code around it did". Those are different jobs, and the second one is mostly verification.

Separating the plan from the typing

I ran this as a pipeline instead of a chat. Four stages, each with a different job and a different amount of room to improvise.

Planning ran at MAX. The output was not code. It was a map: which routes exist, which utilities they share, where the business logic belongs, and in what order to move things so the app never sat in a half state. Writing that map first is the step I would have skipped working alone in an editor. In a chat, the plan lives in the conversation and evaporates when the context does.

Execution ran at HIGH, against the map. Agent A moved the routes out, pulled the utility libraries apart from the business logic, and kept the public handlers pointing at the same shapes. Its mandate was narrow: follow the plan, do not redesign.

That narrowness matters. An executor allowed to improve things while it moves them is doing two refactors at once, and only one of them is being checked.

The reviewer that did not write the code

The third stage is the one I would keep if I could keep only one. A second agent, on a different model, read Agent A's output.

Different model is the point, not a detail. An agent reviewing its own work grades its own assumptions. It re-reads the plan it just followed and finds the plan reasonable. A model that never saw the reasoning has to reconstruct intent from the diff, and that is exactly where the gaps show.

The review caught two kinds of problem. Scope hallucination: code that solved a problem nobody assigned, or a piece that moved when the plan had deliberately left it alone. And syntax-level errors the executor had stopped seeing, the way a typo disappears in a paragraph you have read too many times.

None of it is magic. A reviewer without the plan can also invent objections. What it reliably does is read the code as a stranger, and a stranger does not inherit your tunnel vision.

What the numbers prove

The last stage was verification, and it was narrower than the review. Endpoint validation, plus unit tests over the modules carrying the security rules and the path handling. The final count was 27 tests.

I want to be precise about what 27 means. It is not coverage. It is 27 assertions that the security rules behave as they did before the split, written against the modules where a silent change would have been expensive. The tests prove what they assert. They do not prove the refactor is correct everywhere, and I would not claim that from a number.

The result I care about more is that the public API did not change. Routes, payload shapes and responses stayed where the frontend expected them. That is not a metric. It is a constraint that held for the whole job.

Three files became modules separated by responsibility: routes apart from utilities, utilities apart from business logic. Smaller files are the visible part. The useful part is that the next change has an obvious place to go.

The rule

A refactor is not finished when the files are smaller. It is finished when the contract is unchanged and something can prove it.

The pipeline is how I got there, not the story. Plan at high reasoning, execute against a written map, review with a model that did not write the code, then verify the part where a mistake would cost the most. Each stage catches a different failure, which is why collapsing them into one long conversation undoes the point.

What changed for me is scale, not speed. I did not type 10,000 lines faster. I could hold a structure that size long enough to finish it, because the thinking, the moving and the checking were in separate hands.

entry.title: Naming a tree
entry.summary: TreeList accepted every BaseProps attribute and dropped it before the DOM, so a headerless tree could not be named. The fix was three precedence rules and a test that asserted on the element carrying the role.
entry.content:
A tree without a name is not a tree to a screen reader. It is a shape that opens and closes and never says what it contains.

Last August I merged a fix in Astryx for exactly that. The report looked small: TreeList accepted the same BaseProps as every other component in the library, TypeScript checked the prop, and the tree was still unnamed. The component destructured a fixed set of props with no rest spread, so aria-*, role, tabIndex, id and event handlers were dropped before the DOM. The pull request has the shortest reproduction I know:

render(<TreeList items={items} aria-label="File tree" />);

// <div class="astryx-tree-list ...">
//   <ul role="tree">
// aria-label -> null

The accessibility cost is the sharp one. A tree is named where the tree role is. When the component had a visible header, it generated an id and wired aria-labelledby to it. When it did not, there was no naming path. A screen reader announced "tree" and nothing else. In a file explorer with two trees, a blind user cannot tell which one they are in, and the only way to find out is to open one and listen to what falls out.

The type was the contract, and the type was lying.

Why nothing caught it

TypeScript accepted the prop because TreeListProps extends BaseProps. The header of that type says it keeps aria-*, role, tabIndex, id and event handlers. Nothing warned at runtime: React does not know that aria-label disappeared between the props object and the <ul>.

The accessibility audit on the pull request itself reported no violations. The tree was still unnamed. An unnamed tree is not a missing required attribute; it is a valid tree that happens to be unusable. That is the gap. A linter can tell you whether a role allows an attribute. It cannot tell you whether the thing has a name a person can use.

The first test I wrote made the same mistake. It asserted on container.firstElementChild, the layout <div> that received the spread. The test went green. The <ul role="tree"> still had nothing.

The first review

cixzhang's first review was precise: "The tree still can't be named." aria-label landed on the wrapper div, not on the <ul> that carries role="tree". The screenshot of Chromium's accessibility tree showed the tree with an empty name. My test was asserting on the div I had changed, not on the element that carries the role.

There was a second problem in the same review. I had spread ...restProps after role="tree", so a consumer could pass role="listbox" and displace the contract. The role that makes a tree a tree was optional by accident. The convention in the repo is the opposite: contract props go after the spread, so the component wins. ListItem and Kbd, in the same directory, already spread their rest props. TreeList and List were the exceptions, and the issue listed ten more components with the same shape. One omission copied.

I had it backwards in two places at once: the spread order and the test target.

The second review

The next version pulled aria-label and aria-labelledby out of the rest and put them on the <ul role="tree">. It also wrote role="tree" after the spread. The tree could be named. The role was stable.

Then cixzhang asked for one more thing: when TreeList renders a visible header, the generated header id should keep naming the tree. My version let a caller aria-labelledby replace it, so assistive technology could hear a different name than the one on screen. That is a quiet failure. The visible label and the announced label diverge, and the person reading the screen and the person listening to it are no longer in the same document.

The fix was a precedence rule: if a visible header exists, its id wins; a caller label only applies on the headerless path. I added tests for both paths and asserted on getByRole('tree'), not on the wrapper. The List half was left to the maintainers so the same work was not done twice.

What the fix did not do is invent a default name. "Tree" is not a name; it is the role said twice. The component cannot know what the tree contains. It had to expose the name the caller already had, and then get out of the way.

The rule

Name the element that carries the role. Test the element that carries the role. A wrapper is not the thing.

A visible label outranks a programmatic one, because the two have to describe the same object. And a contract prop belongs after the spread: the component owns the semantics that make it what it is.

The lesson of the ten other components is not that ten components are broken. It is that a missing convention propagates: one omission gets copied, and every copy looks correct in review because the type says it is. The fix is not a patch per component. It is the house pattern, written down and tested where the role lives.

Five regression tests, and the tree has a name now. That is the whole product.

entry.title: When a HoverCard calls itself a dialog
entry.summary: A labelled HoverCard trigger described itself with aria-describedby, so screen reader users heard the card's contents as a description instead of learning that a dialog opens. The fix is the popup contract, with two review catches along the way.
entry.content:
A HoverCard with a label was a dialog that never said so. The trigger pointed at it with aria-describedby, so the first thing a screen reader user heard about the card was its contents, flattened into a description of the button.

The report was issue 5049, and the fix is PR 5419, merged in August. One component, four files. The interesting part is not the list of attributes. It is the difference between describing a thing and opening one.

The trigger that described the card

The reproduction in the issue is short:

<HoverCard
  label="Profile actions"
  content={<Button onClick={handleFollow}>Follow</Button>}>
  <button type="button">Jane Doe</button>
</HoverCard>

Focus the trigger, "Jane Doe". The card renders role="dialog" with aria-label="Profile actions". The trigger carries aria-describedby pointing at that layer.

So the screen reader reads the button's name, then reads the dialog's content as its description. Structure collapses into a string. What the person does not hear is that a dialog opens.

Two costs follow. The user cannot tell there is anything to open, because a description does not invite interaction. And the content they did hear arrives before they asked for it, with no region to navigate, no boundary, no way to move inside it. The card can contain a button, links, anything focusable. A non-modal dialog is the right model for that. A description is the model for one supplementary sentence.

The lazy context layer work made it worse. While the card is closed, the layer is not in the DOM at all, only an inert <template> marker carrying the id. The trigger's aria-describedby pointed there too. Closed, the trigger referenced an empty sentinel. Open, the same attribute pointed at a dialog with focusable content. One attribute, two meanings, and neither of them "a popup opens here".

Why nothing caught it

Every check passed. The attribute is valid, the id resolves, the props type accepts the value, React renders what the component asked for.

The automated accessibility audit on the pull request reported no violations. That is the gap worth naming. Audits check that relationships exist and attributes are allowed in a role. A trigger correctly described by a dialog breaks no rule. It is a wrong model written in legal ARIA.

A diff review does not catch it either unless the reviewer holds the screen reader model in their head. The new markup looks more complete than the old one: there is a describedby, a role, a label. Complete and wrong are compatible. That is why the fix needed an argument about semantics, not a lint rule.

The contract

Two relationships, two jobs.

aria-describedby says: here is more text about this control. It is a string, flattened, read in place, before the person decides to go anywhere.

aria-haspopup="dialog" says: this control opens a dialog. aria-expanded says whether it is open now. aria-controls points at the element being controlled, and only while that element exists.

The fix applies the second contract when there is a label:

  • aria-haspopup="dialog" on the trigger
  • aria-expanded synced to the open state
  • aria-controls set to the layer id only while the card is open, cleared or restored when it closes

That last condition came from matching what DateInput already does in the same library. An aria-controls that names an id missing from the DOM is a reference to nothing. Nothing crashes, no audit flags it, and assistive technology gets an unreliable map of the page.

I also exposed id and isOpen from useHoverCard, so a consumer driving the hook directly can wire the same contract, and kept describedBy as a deprecated alias of id so existing call sites keep working.

Then the case the fix does not cover. With no label, the card renders role="group" and the trigger keeps aria-describedby. aria-haspopup="dialog" over an unnamed group would promise a dialog and deliver something else. The naming decision for unlabelled rich cards is still open in 5049. I left it there rather than guess a default.

aria-details was the other candidate and I did not use it. Screen reader support is still uneven, and the attribute is built for pointing at a larger body of content, not at an interactive surface that opens and closes. aria-haspopup plus aria-expanded is the contract more assistive technology actually implements for a non-modal dialog opener.

The review, and the third bug

cixzhang's first review requested changes, and both objections were correct.

The hook example in the docs put aria-haspopup="dialog" on a trigger whose card had no label. In Chrome the button announced "has dialog popup" and then opened an unnamed group. My own change had produced the exact mismatch I was fixing, inside the code I wrote to demonstrate it. Passing label: 'Alex Morgan' in the example closed that hole.

The second was worse. On the labelled path I wrote the trigger's aria-haspopup, aria-controls and aria-expanded, then removed them on cleanup. Wrap a menu button in a labelled HoverCard and its menu semantics disappear, silently, with nothing left to say they were there. Fifteen lines below, the no-label branch merged with existing values and restored them. One branch had the right pattern and I did not carry it across.

The rewrite reads the trigger's existing attributes, merges aria-controls with the layer id, and restores all three on cleanup. I added a test that wraps a menu button, with its own popup attributes, inside a labelled HoverCard.

There was a third problem I found while fixing those two. aria-controls pointed at the layer id even when the layer was not in the DOM. I gated it on the open state, the way DateInput does.

The final diff is 168 additions and 10 deletions across four files, with 38 tests in HoverCard.test.tsx, typecheck and build passing. The reviewer verified in Chrome that a menu trigger keeps its own semantics and gets them back after cleanup, then merged.

The rule

A control that opens something has to say that before it says what is inside.

Describing and opening are different promises and one attribute cannot carry both. If the thing on the other side is a navigable region, the trigger owes the user a relationship and a state, not a paragraph of somebody else's content read out of turn.

And when two branches of the same effect touch the same attributes, both merge and restore. One branch that overwrites is enough to make the component own semantics it did not create.

The follow-up went after a different version of the same problem in List and TreeList: attributes that never reached the DOM at all.

entry.title: aria-orientation belongs to the role owner
entry.summary: A Combobox with grid rendered aria-orientation on role=grid, which does not support it. The attribute moved to the components that assign the role; the keyboard hook kept only the behavior.
entry.content:
A missing attribute is easy to catch. Nothing renders, a test fails, someone fills the hole. The expensive bug is the attribute that renders in the wrong place, where it is valid HTML, valid TypeScript, and still a contradiction.

In August I merged mui/base-ui #5551 for one of those. A Combobox with grid enabled rendered this:

<div role="grid" aria-orientation="horizontal">

Both halves are legal on their own. Together they describe two different widgets.

The reproduction was the official emoji picker in the Autocomplete grid example: open the list, inspect the element, find role="grid" and aria-orientation="horizontal" on the same node, run axe. Nothing looked broken. The picker opened, the arrows moved, the emoji inserted.

Two instructions at once

role="grid" is a two-dimensional structure. It has rows and columns, and arrow keys move through both axes. aria-orientation="horizontal" says the widget runs along a single line. A person navigating with a screen reader hears position by row and column, then gets an attribute claiming the thing is a strip.

That is the difference between a bug that removes information and one that adds noise. A missing label leaves a silence you can notice. A contradiction leaves a sentence that sounds complete and is wrong, and the person on the other end has no way to tell which half to trust.

The spec resolves the conflict by dropping the attribute. WAI-ARIA 1.2 requires user agents to ignore non-global properties on roles that do not support them, so grid never receives aria-orientation. That is not a repair. The component published an intent it could not express, the intent vanished at the accessibility tree, and the keyboard kept working because the keyboard logic never read the attribute in the first place.

Axe found it as an aria-allowed-attr violation, reported against the official Autocomplete grid example on v1.7.0, with axe-core 4.10.2. A tool caught it. The component's own suite did not, because no test asked which element carried the role.

Why the type said yes

aria-orientation is a valid prop on any React element. TypeScript checks the name and the value, "horizontal" | "vertical" | undefined. It cannot check the role of the node the prop reaches, because at the point of the check there is no node.

The attribute was assembled inside useListNavigation, returned in a props object, and spread later onto whichever element ended up with the role. In the source, the attribute and the role never meet. They only meet in the DOM, and only a tool that inspects the rendered tree sees them together.

The type was doing its job. It was checking the wrong contract.

One variable, two jobs

The root cause was a coupling. AriaCombobox passed orientation: grid ? 'horizontal' : undefined into useListNavigation, and the hook exposed any orientation other than 'both' as aria-orientation. The hook genuinely needed horizontal: it drives ArrowLeft and ArrowRight inside a grid. It then treated that keyboard requirement as a reason to publish ARIA.

That is the wrong owner. A navigation hook knows how keys should move. It does not know what role its consumer will render, and it should not guess.

Three public components sit on that hook. The Combobox, the Menu and the Select each pass an orientation and each render a different role. One emission, three roles, and only one of them rejects the attribute outright. The other two accept it and do not need it.

So the fix took the emission out of the hook, two deleted lines, and moved the attribute to the components that assign the final role. MenuRoot renders aria-orientation="horizontal" only when the menu is horizontal, because menu is implicitly vertical. SelectPopup dropped a dead 'aria-orientation': undefined from its presentation branch. Grid and listbox get nothing: a grid is two-dimensional, a listbox is implicitly vertical, and saying either out loud adds nothing.

Seven files, 69 lines added, 4 removed. Three of those additions are production code. The other 66 are tests: the Combobox grid and listbox, the generic hook, a horizontal and a vertical menu, a select listbox.

The ratio is the honest one. The change is small and the proof is not.

The tests query by role, getByRole('grid') and getByRole('listbox'), then assert the attribute is absent. Not by container, not by test id. That is the check that was missing: an assertion about the node a screen reader will actually read, in place of an assertion about the node the props happened to reach.

The third time

The issue pointed at two earlier fixes of the same shape: #4355 for Navigation Menu, #4628 for Toggle Group. Same invalid attribute, different component, same hook underneath.

That is the part I kept returning to. Each fix was correct where it landed, and the generator stayed. As long as the shared hook emitted the attribute, every new consumer inherited the bug, and every reviewer had to notice it again on a different component. A patch per component is a tax paid forever.

What would have prevented the third one is a convention, not a fix: ARIA that depends on a role belongs to the component that assigns the role. Hooks return behavior. Components publish semantics. Once that line is drawn, the question "does this role support this attribute" has an obvious place to be answered.

The rule

An attribute is not valid in the abstract. It is valid for a role, on an element. When the thing that decides the role is not the thing that decides the attribute, the contract has no owner, and no type will tell you.

Read the attribute from the element that carries the role, not from the props object that produced it.

entry.title: A breadcrumb that does not rely on color
entry.summary: Astryx marked the current breadcrumb item with a slightly darker gray and nothing else, failing WCAG 1.4.1. The fix was one font-weight declaration, and the trade was a few pixels of width.
entry.content:
A breadcrumb is a map. If the only thing marking your position on that map is a shade of gray, then for some people the map has no dot on it.

I spent three weeks of calendar time on two lines in a style object. One of them was the fix.

Two grays

In Astryx, the links in a breadcrumb trail render in --color-text-secondary. The current page renders in --color-text-primary. Same font, same size, same row, same separator between items. The only thing telling "you can go here" apart from "you are here" was a small step in luminance.

Most people read that step without noticing they read it. A cue that works for almost everyone stops looking like a cue.

For a person with low vision, or a lens that has yellowed, or a laptop screen at noon on a terrace, the two grays compress toward each other. The step becomes a rumor. And in forced-colors mode the browser replaces author colors outright, so both items resolve to the same system color and the distinction disappears completely. Not reduced. Gone.

Here is the part that took me a while to name correctly. Screen reader users were fine. aria-current="page" was already on the current item, and assistive technology announced it as the current page. The semantic layer was correct. The failure lived entirely in the visual layer, and only for the people who depend on that layer without getting the color part of it. An accessibility attribute did not save a visual-only cue, because it was never meant to.

Why nothing caught it

The accessibility audit that runs on every pull request reported, on mine, "No accessibility violations detected." That was true and useless at the same time.

Tools like axe measure contrast ratio between text and background. Both grays pass, because both are readable text on a light surface. Neither one is a contrast violation. The question in WCAG 1.4.1 is different: is color the only visual means of conveying this information? That is a question about a pair of states and what distinguishes them, not about a single ratio. No linter reads that intent, and no automated pass can answer it.

The issue had been open since July 27, filed by chris-gds, labeled an accessibility bug and tracked in the program tracker. Its body names the exposure plainly: products built on the design system fail standard audits, with legal weight under the ADA and the European Accessibility Act, and it is marked High / Blocker. I did not find that by being clever. I found the two tokens while reading the component, and the report was already there with a screenshot and a severity label.

Severity labels do not merge code. That is the whole distance between a filed bug and a fixed one.

One declaration, three weeks

The fix is font-weight: var(--font-weight-semibold) on the shared current style. Value 600. Because the style object is shared, it covers both the default variant and the supporting variant, which is the one the audit was pointing at.

The aria-current="page" stayed exactly where it was. I did not touch it, and I did not need to. The visual channel got a second signal, and the announcement channel kept the signal it already had.

Two lines added, one removed, one file changed. That is the entire product.

The first version of my pull request deserved to be closed.

My branch carried commits from separate color-contrast work, which had its own pull request open. Unrelated changes had leaked in, and a reviewer looking at that diff would have had no way to know which part was the breadcrumb fix and which part belonged somewhere else. Scope is the first thing a reviewer reads.

So I rebased onto main, cut the branch down to exactly one change, and re-verified the whole surface: 25 of 25 tests in the Breadcrumbs suite, lint clean, check:sync clean, package boundaries clean. All of that was already green before, and none of it had caught the bug. I ran it anyway, because after a rebase the only thing you own is the evidence.

Then the repository did something I did not expect. The Breadcrumbs audit, a separate piece of work with its own findings, hit the same problem as finding B8 and explicitly deferred it to my open pull request instead of landing a color-only patch that would have collided with the proper fix. The audit named the issue, named the PR, and named the approach: semibold weight on the shared current style.

A queue of audits is not usually a friend to a contributor. This one was.

What the weight costs

cixzhang approved it with one nit that I kept: semibold runs about four pixels wider, so long labels wrap sooner.

That is the honest price of the fix, and it is small enough to pay. Every non-color cue costs something. An underline would fight the link underline in the same row and blur the affordance instead of sharpening it. A border would put a box around plain text and invent a container the design does not have. An icon would require a new asset, a decision about which glyph means "current", and a translation of that glyph for every locale. Weight was the channel already present in the type system, and it costs layout instead of vocabulary.

It also raises the current item's visual rank, which is the direction you want. The place you are should not read as the quietest thing in the row.

What it does not do is make the breadcrumb better for screen readers, because that part was never broken. And if the loaded font has no 600 cut, the browser synthesizes one or picks the nearest weight, and the cue gets thinner than the declaration promises. A second channel is still a channel, not a guarantee.

The rule

Desaturate the component and look at it. If the states collapse into one, you never had a second channel. You had color and a story about color.

That test takes a screenshot and ten seconds, and it catches the class of bug that ships under a green audit. It is not a substitute for testing with assistive technology. It is the test that asks whether the thing is visible at all to someone who is not you.

The merge landed at 00:48 on August 24, twenty four days after I opened the PR. Two lines in the diff, three weeks in the calendar, and a trail that still points at you when the colors go away.
